title: Three Separate Windows With the Top Sum
statement:
You get an array of positive integers nums and a window length k. Choose three windows, each exactly k consecutive elements long, that do not overlap. Make the total of all elements inside them as large as possible.

Return the three starting indices in increasing order. If several choices reach the same largest total, return the one that is lexicographically smallest: the smallest first index, then the smallest second index, then the smallest third.

examples.why: Windows [2, 1], [2, 6], [2, 2] total 15. Starting the first window at 1 gives the same total, but 0 comes first.
Every choice totals 15; the earliest one wins the tie.
Grabbing the best window [7, 7] first leaves [2, 1] and [1, 1] for the others (total 19). Splitting the 7s into [2, 7] and [7, 2] gives 20.

hints: First turn the problem into one about window sums: W[i] is the sum of the window starting at i. Now pick three indices at least k apart.
Fix the middle window at j. The best left window lies anywhere in 0 … j − k, and the best right window anywhere in j + k … end. Those two choices are independent.
Precompute, for every position, the index of the best window up to it from the left and from it to the right. Keep the earliest index on ties so the answer comes out lexicographically smallest.

explain.intuition:
Greedy fails: taking the biggest window first can block two good windows, as in the third example. But once the middle window is fixed at j, the left and right windows no longer interact: the left one is simply the best window ending before j, and the right one is the best window starting after j + k − 1.

So precompute window sums with a sliding sum, then two arrays: left[i], the index of the best window starting in 0 … i, and right[i], the best starting in i … m − 1. Try every middle and keep the best total. Ties need care: left only moves on a strictly bigger sum, right moves on bigger or equal (it scans from the right, so equal means further left), and the middle loop only replaces the answer on a strictly bigger total.
steps: Compute W[i] = sum of nums[i … i + k − 1] for i = 0 … m − 1, m = n − k + 1.
left[i]: start at 0; for each i, use i if W[i] > W[left[i − 1]], else keep left[i − 1].
right[i]: start at m − 1; going left, use i if W[i] ≥ W[right[i + 1]].
For each middle j from k to m − 1 − k: total = W[left[j − k]] + W[j] + W[right[j + k]]. Replace the answer only if strictly larger.
pitfalls: Picking the largest window first and then the best of what is left. See the third example.
Using > in the right-to-left scan. On a tie it keeps the later index and returns a lexicographically larger answer.
Letting the left window end inside the middle one: the left window must start at most at j − k.

solutions.title: Try every triple of window starts
solutions.idea: Compute window sums, then check all a < b < c spaced at least k apart in increasing order, keeping the first strictly best.

solutions.title: Best left, best right, scan the middle
solutions.idea: Precompute the best window index on each side of every position, then try each middle window once.

followups: Generalise to t windows instead of three. What does a DP over (windows used, position) look like?
Return only the largest total, with no tie-breaking. Which parts of the solution become simpler?
